Context quality determines agent quality. MicroClaw uses layered context management to keep long conversations useful and bounded.

Live turn context: latest user input + immediate tool outputs. Session history: persisted conversation blocks (including tool_use/tool_result). Compacted summary context: when session grows beyond threshold. File memory: AGENTS.md global + bot + per-chat memory (written by write_memory tool). Structured memories: rows extracted from the memories table by the background Reflector.

Load session from sessions table when available. Append new user messages since updated_at. Inject memory context: file memory (AGENTS.md) + structured memories from DB. If message count exceeds max_session_messages, compact older blocks. Run tool loop, then persist updated session state. Structured memory injection is budgeted by memory_token_budget (default 1500, estimated as content.len()/4 + 10 per memory). When budget is hit, remaining rows are omitted and a summary suffix is appended.

Runs independently of the main chat loop every reflector_interval_mins (default 15 min). For each chat it tracks a cursor in memory_reflector_state, processes only unseen messages, calls the LLM to extract structured facts, validates categories, deduplicates, and persists to the memories table. This decouples memory extraction from model attention while avoiding repeated scans. Dedup mode: semantic mode: sqlite-vec feature + runtime embedding config fallback mode: Jaccard similarity See Memory System for details.

Before each model call the conversation is measured against the model's context window (context_window.rs: known models by name, model_context_window(s) overrides, the reply reserve subtracted). Compaction starts at context_pressure_compact_pct (at most 90%) of that budget, when a chat exceeds max_session_messages, or after a provider "context length exceeded" error, and runs in stages: Prune (no model call): older tool outputs are replaced by a one-line stub naming the call; the newest prune_protect_tokens of tool output stay, and pruning only happens when it frees at least prune_minimum_tokens, so the provider's prompt cache is not invalidated for small gains. A read_file result superseded by a later read of the same file is always replaced. Spilled outputs keep their fetch_artifact id. Summarize: if still over budget, older history (everything before the kept tail of compact_keep_recent messages or compact_keep_recent_tokens tokens, always starting on a plain user message) is summarized into fixed sections: goal and constraints, decisions, files and state, errors and fixes, plan, verification, next step. The previous summary is updated incrementally; long histories are summarized in chunks. Re-inject: the summary message also carries the user's own earlier messages verbatim and the files changed, so constraints survive. Fallback: if the summarizer fails, a mechanical digest (earlier summary, user requests, files changed, last commands) replaces the history instead of dropping it. A turn stops compacting after two attempts that cannot reduce further. Every compaction archives the full conversation first and emits a context_compacted runtime event. Images are stripped before session persistence.

At prompt build time, structured memories are ordered by: semantic KNN (sqlite-vec + configured embedding provider) fallback keyword relevance scoring (CJK-aware tokenizer) with recency tie-break MCP-backed query ordering when a memory MCP backend is active (memory_query + memory_upsert) When MCP memory backend is active, local sqlite-vec KNN ranking is not applied to MCP-backed rows; query ordering comes from MCP results, with automatic SQLite fallback on MCP failures.

Current model: Sub-agent runs use a restricted tool registry via ToolRegistry::new_sub_agent. Session-native async runs are created with sessions_spawn and managed with subagents_* tools. Spawn depth is bounded by subagents.max_spawn_depth and defaults to 1, so nested delegation is opt-in and capped. Child runs do not receive the full side-effect surface from the main agent registry. Recommended next step: Explicit inheritance policy by field (history, memory, tool results, working_dir). Context provenance markers in debug output.
Use: RUST_LOG=debug cargo run -- start Web stream/tool events for per-iteration tool traces. microclaw doctor for environment/dependency issues that often masquerade as context problems.
MCP extends tool surface area without baking all integrations into MicroClaw itself.

Supported transports: stdio streamable_http Protocol version is negotiated during initialize (default currently 2024-11-05, configurable per server/global). Config sources are merged from: <data_dir>/mcp.json <data_dir>/mcp.d/*.json (filename order; later files override earlier definitions for the same server key)
request timeout (request_timeout_secs) retry + reconnect for stdio (max_retries) tools cache with TTL + forced refresh periodic health probe (health_interval_secs, 0 disables)

MCP tools are registered into the same runtime tool registry with namespaced identifiers. This keeps planner behavior consistent between built-in tools and MCP tools. Additionally, MicroClaw can use MCP as a structured-memory backend when a server exposes: memory_query memory_upsert In that mode, memory operations become MCP-first with automatic fallback to local SQLite on per-call failures. Minimal config sketch: { "mcpServers": { "memory": { "transport": "streamable_http", "endpoint": "http://127.0.0.1:8090/mcp" } } } This server is considered memory-capable only when it exposes both memory_query and memory_upsert.

Start with minimal local MCP config. Add remote servers one-by-one. Monitor tool list refresh and probe failures in logs. Treat endpoint auth and command dependencies as first-class operational dependencies.
Skills provide workflow intelligence without hardcoding every domain behavior into the core engine.

A skill is a directory with SKILL.md frontmatter + instructions. Required/important metadata: name description platforms (optional, filtered) deps (optional command checks) source / version / updated_at (for provenance)
Skill catalog is surfaced in system prompt. Agent calls activate_skill only when needed. Platform/dependency filters hide incompatible skills from runtime catalog.
builtin: shipped with MicroClaw data bootstrap. local: user-authored skill in local skills directory. remote: synchronized via sync_skills and normalized locally.

Core framework should provide: discovery metadata parsing/validation activation APIs compatibility filtering Core framework should not embed domain-specific business workflows. Those belong in skills.

Emoji reaction reply is supported: If the model final response is a single emoji/emoji token (for example 👍, :thumbsdown:, TearsofJoy), MicroClaw sends Feishu reaction on the original message. Supports direct emoji_type values and common aliases/emoji characters (including Chinese aliases like 点赞). For finer control, model output can use: reaction-only: <emoji-or-token> for reaction only. reaction: <emoji-or-token> + newline + reply text for reaction + text. [reaction: <emoji-or-token>] <reply text> as inline form. If reaction send fails: implicit single-token reaction output falls back to plain text. explicit reaction-only: keeps silent text-wise (no forced text reply).

Full supported emoji_type set is maintained in code: src/channels/feishu.rs (FEISHU_EMOJI_TYPES). Current built-in list size: 254 emoji types. The bot can choose any supported emoji_type directly (for example THUMBSUP, PARTY, ROCKET). No fixed meaning mapping is enforced. MicroClaw Code is a coding agent for your own repository. You describe a change; it reads the code, edits files (showing every diff), runs commands and your project's checks, and fixes what fails. It runs on your machine, with your toolchain. We recommend using it in Zed: MicroClaw Code appears in Zed's Agent Panel next to Zed's own agent, with diffs you can review in the editor, approval cards, mode and model pickers and a context meter. The same agent also runs in your terminal, with a full-screen interface or mccode -p for scripts and CI. Both use the same sessions and settings. In Zed through the Agent Client Protocol: edits as real diffs, checks as cards, / commands, thread history (set up). In the terminal: a full-screen UI with streamed replies, coloured diffs, plans and approval dialogs, or mccode -p for scripts and CI. Three permission modes: plan (read-only, proposes a plan), ask (edits apply, shell commands ask first), auto (commands run, destructive ones still ask). Verification built in: after a change it runs your build, lint and test commands and hands failures back to the agent. Safety by default: shell commands run in the operating system's sandbox, edits are checkpointed (/undo), and project settings only take effect after you trust the project. Works with other agents too: any Agent Client Protocol editor through mccode acp, and Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other MCP clients through mccode mcp-server. One engine: the same Agent Engine as MicroClaw Server and the Rust SDK, so tools, memory, Skills and model providers behave the same everywhere. Status: Preview.

curl -fsSL https://microclaw.org/install-mccode.sh | bash The script downloads mccode for your platform from the latest GitHub release, verifies it against the release's SHA256SUMS.txt, and installs it to /usr/local/bin (or ~/.local/bin when that is not writable). Options: curl -fsSL https://microclaw.org/install-mccode.sh | bash -s -- --version 0.29.0 curl -fsSL https://microclaw.org/install-mccode.sh | bash -s -- --dir ~/bin
iwr https://microclaw.org/install-mccode.ps1 -UseBasicParsing | iex This installs mccode.exe to %USERPROFILE%\.local\bin and adds that folder to your user PATH.
brew install microclaw/tap/mccode

Needs the Rust toolchain: cargo install --git https://github.com/microclaw/microclaw microclaw-code Releases before 0.25.0 have no mccode archives; asked for one of those, the installers print this command instead.

mccode update # install the latest release (checksum-verified) mccode update --check # only report whether a newer release exists Homebrew installs update with brew upgrade mccode. To uninstall, delete the mccode binary (and ~/.mccode to remove settings and sessions).

mccode setup setup asks for a provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Ollama and the other providers MicroClaw supports), a model and an API key, and writes ~/.mccode/config.yaml (readable only by you). For scripts: mccode setup --provider anthropic --model claude-sonnet-4-5 --api-key "$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" mccode setup --provider ollama --model qwen3-coder --base-url http://127.0.0.1:11434/v1 A model profile in ~/.mccode/settings.yaml works instead of that file (see settings), and --config <PATH> or MCCODE_CONFIG names another configuration file. mccode never uses a MicroClaw Server configuration, and a microclaw.config.yaml inside a repository is never loaded, so a cloned project cannot choose your model endpoint. Check everything with: mccode doctor

Install Zed, a free, open-source editor. Download it from zed.dev/download, or use your package manager: brew install --cask zed # macOS (12 or later) curl -f https://zed.dev/install.sh | sh # Linux (needs a Vulkan 1.3 driver) winget install -e --id ZedIndustries.Zed # Windows (10 version 1903 or later, 64-bit) Find where mccode is installed: which mccode # for example /Users/you/.local/bin/mccode In Zed, open the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+P elsewhere), run zed: open settings and add MicroClaw Code as an agent, using that path: { "agent_servers": { "MicroClaw Code": { "type": "custom", "command": "/Users/you/.local/bin/mccode", "args": ["acp"] } } } Open your repository in Zed, open the Agent Panel, click + and choose MicroClaw Code. Type a task, mention files with @, and approve commands on the cards that appear. The Zed integration described in these docs (mode and model pickers, real diffs, permission cards, thread history) needs mccode 0.27.0 or later; check with mccode --version and update with mccode update. For trusting a project, the options above, what each part of the panel shows and troubleshooting, see Use with Zed.

cd path/to/your/repo mccode If the repository has a .microclaw/project.yaml or detectable checks, mccode asks whether you trust it. Trusting lets the project's settings and checks run; you can change it later with /trust. Type a task, for example add a --verbose flag to the CLI and a test for it. Mention files with @path (Tab completes them). Watch the agent read, edit (each change is shown as a diff) and run commands. In ask mode a shell command opens an approval dialog: 1 approve once, 2 always allow the tool, p always allow that command in this project, 3 deny. After the change, your project's checks run automatically; failures go back to the agent for a bounded number of fix rounds. Not happy? /undo restores the files to before that turn. /review asks for a review of everything uncommitted. Start with /plan <task> to get a plan first, and Shift+Tab to switch between plan, ask and auto. One task without the full-screen interface: mccode -p "fix the failing parser test"

Everything MicroClaw Code stores is in ~/.mccode (override with MCCODE_HOME): the model configuration, the engine database and memory, checkpoints, the session index, trust decisions and allow rules. MicroClaw Code and the MicroClaw Server are separate products: each installs, updates and uninstalls on its own, and neither reads the other's configuration, data or environment variables. Pairing with a Server (mccode remote pair) is the only link, and only when you set it up.

Use with Zed: the full Zed guide, other ACP editors, and MCP clients such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Using MicroClaw Code: modes, approvals, the sandbox, verification, sessions, scripting and evaluation. Run tasks on a MicroClaw Server.

Zed is the recommended way to use MicroClaw Code. Zed runs it in its Agent Panel, next to Zed's own agent, and shows its edits as diffs you can review in the editor. The terminal interface stays available for the same sessions. Besides Zed, mccode speaks two protocols on stdio, so other programs can use it without the terminal interface: Command Protocol For mccode acp Agent Client Protocol Editors with an agent panel: Zed, and other ACP clients mccode mcp-server Model Context Protocol Other agents: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, any MCP client Both use the same engine, settings, trust decisions and sessions as the terminal interface. Install mccode and run mccode setup first (see Overview and install); check the result with mccode doctor.

Zed runs external agents through ACP and shows them in its Agent Panel. Version This guide describes mccode 0.27.0 and later. Check with mccode --version and update with mccode update (or brew upgrade mccode).

Zed is a free, open-source editor for macOS, Linux and Windows. Download it from zed.dev/download, or install it from a terminal: System Command Requirements macOS brew install --cask zed macOS 12 or later Linux curl -f https://zed.dev/install.sh | sh x86_64 or aarch64, Vulkan 1.3 driver Windows winget install -e --id ZedIndustries.Zed Windows 10 version 1903 or later, 64-bit MicroClaw Code needs no Zed account: it uses your own model configuration.

Find the installed binary with which mccode (on Windows, where.exe mccode), then open Zed's settings and add the entry below. Either run zed: open settings from the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS, Ctrl+Shift+P elsewhere), or run agent: open settings, go to External Agents and choose Add Agent → Add Custom Agent, which opens the same file with an empty entry. The settings file is ~/.config/zed/settings.json on macOS and Linux. { "agent_servers": { "MicroClaw Code": { "type": "custom", "command": "/Users/you/.local/bin/mccode", "args": ["acp"], "env": {} } } } Use the full path: Zed started from the Dock or the desktop does not read your shell profile, so a bare mccode is often not found. On Windows write it with escaped backslashes, for example "C:\\Users\\you\\.local\\bin\\mccode.exe". Older Zed releases do not know "type"; leave that line out there. Global options go before acp: "args": ["--mode", "auto", "--no-network", "acp"] Useful ones: --mode plan|ask|auto (starting mode), --no-network, --sandbox off, --no-verify, --config <PATH> (model settings). env passes environment variables, for example "MCCODE_HOME": "/path/to/another/home" or an API key referenced by your configuration.
documents.s: 2. Add MicroClaw Code as an agent

documents.t: Open a folder that is (inside) a git repository. Open the Agent Panel, click + and choose MicroClaw Code. Type a task. Mention files with @ as in Zed's own agent, or add files, symbols, images or the branch diff with the + button under the message box; their content is sent along with the prompt. Each Zed thread is a MicroClaw Code session in the project of the folder Zed opened. The thread is named after your first message (or the attached file when you typed nothing), appears in Zed's thread history, and reopening it loads the session and replays its messages. Threads started in Zed and sessions started in the terminal are the same sessions (mccode sessions lists both); Import Threads in Zed's thread list brings in sessions you started in the terminal or in other projects. If no model is configured yet, Zed asks you to sign in: choose Set up MicroClaw Code and Zed runs mccode setup in a terminal. Afterwards start the thread again.

Mode and model: the selectors under the message box switch between Plan (read-only, proposes a plan), Ask (edits apply, commands ask) and Auto (commands run, destructive ones still ask), and between the models of the session's provider (your settings profile's models and the known models of the same provider). Zed remembers the model you pick. Tool calls: reads, searches and commands appear as tool cards with their status and output; cards carry absolute paths, so Zed can follow the agent. Edits: each edit shows a real diff of the file (old and new text), which Zed renders like its own agent's edits. Checks: in trusted projects the project's checks run after a change and appear as their own cards (Check tests: …) with the result; failures go back to the agent for a fix round, as in the terminal. Plan: the agent's todo list is shown as Zed's plan view and updates as steps complete. Permission requests: when a command needs approval, Zed shows a card with the command and the options Approve once, Always allow the tool in this thread, Always allow this command in this project (single simple commands such as cargo test) and Deny. The agent waits for your answer and continues in the same run. Context: the ring next to the mode picker shows how much of the model's context window the session uses; hover it for the numbers (for example 1% · 14k / 1M). /cost reports requests and tokens, and the estimated cost when the model's price is known. Commands: type / for these, plus your custom commands (~/.mccode/commands, .microclaw/commands in trusted projects): /goal [--until <command>] [--rounds N] <objective>: keep working, round after round, in one run until the goal is met (see Code usage); the stop button ends it; /review [focus], /check [names], /diff [full]: review, run the project's checks, or show the uncommitted changes; /btw <question>: a side question that does not enter the conversation; /undo, /rewind [N]: undo the last turn's file changes, or list the turns and restore files to before turn N; /compact [focus], /cost, /context, /status: context, usage and what the session runs with; /export [path], /init, /help: write the conversation as Markdown, write .microclaw/project.yaml, list the commands. Trust stays a terminal decision (mccode trust, below). Stop: Zed's stop button cancels the run.

Editors cannot show the trust question, so .microclaw/project.yaml (mode, instructions, checks) and AGENTS.md only apply to projects you have already trusted. Trust a project once from a terminal: cd path/to/repo mccode trust # or open `mccode` and answer the question If the file changes later (for example after a pull), trust it again.

Run dev: open acp logs in Zed's command palette to see the messages between Zed and mccode. Run mccode doctor in the same folder: it validates the model configuration and starts the engine once. "command not found" or the agent never starts: use the absolute path in command. No model configured: run mccode setup (or use Zed's sign-in prompt), add a profile to ~/.mccode/settings.yaml, or pass --config <PATH> in args.

Any ACP client works the same way: configure an agent that runs mccode with the argument acp (global options before it) in the project's folder. The client must send the project directory as the session's cwd.

mccode mcp-server exposes two tools: Tool Arguments What it does run prompt, optional cwd, mode (plan/ask/auto), session Runs a coding task in the repository of cwd, with verification and fix rounds. Returns the answer, the changed files, the check result and the session id. review optional focus, cwd Reviews the uncommitted changes (git diff HEAD plus untracked files) with read-only tools and returns findings by severity with file:line. Approvals: a command that needs one ends the run call and says so. Answer by calling run again with the same session and the prompt 1 (approve once), 2 (always allow the tool) or 3 (deny). Use mode: "auto" to avoid most approvals.
documents.s: Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other MCP clients

documents.t: claude mcp add mccode -- mccode mcp-server Add --scope project to share the entry with the repository's .mcp.json. Then ask, for example, "use mccode to fix the failing parser test" or "ask mccode to review my changes".
In ~/.codex/config.toml: [mcp_servers.mccode] command = "mccode" args = ["mcp-server"]
In ~/.cursor/mcp.json (or .cursor/mcp.json in a project): { "mcpServers": { "mccode": { "command": "mccode", "args": ["mcp-server"] } } }

Any MCP client that starts stdio servers works with command mccode and argument mcp-server. Global options go before the subcommand (mccode --mode auto mcp-server). Projects you trusted honour their .microclaw/project.yaml and run their checks; untrusted projects run no checks.

mccode can send a task to a MicroClaw Server instead of running it locally. The task then runs on the Server's machine, in its working directory, with its tools, model and approval policy; mccode streams the result back. This is useful when the code, credentials or hardware live on another machine.
documents.s: Run tasks on a MicroClaw Server

documents.t: On the Server, open the web console, go to Access and create a pairing code. On your machine: mccode remote pair https://server.example.com <code> mccode remote status # shows the paired Server Pairing trades the single-use code for a device token. The token is stored in ~/.mccode/remote.json (readable only by you) and can be revoked from the Server's Access tab. mccode remote forget deletes it locally.

mccode -p "run the nightly data check and summarise failures" --remote mccode -p "…" --remote --json # runtime events as JSON Lines The output and exit codes are the same as for a local -p run; Ctrl+C cancels the run on the Server. Runs from the same folder share one Server session (mccode-<folder name>), so a follow-up task sees the earlier conversation. Pick another one with --session <key>; -p - reads the task from stdin.

When the Server's policy needs a person for a command, the run stops with exit code 2 and prints the session key. Answer it with: mccode -p 1 --remote --session <key> # approve once mccode -p 3 --remote --session <key> # deny The Server's own approval rules apply; local permission modes, allow rules and the local sandbox do not.

mccode reads one settings format from four layers. Use it for the model and per-role models, permission rules, the sandbox's network access, hooks, the look of the terminal interface, key bindings and notifications.

Layer File Notes user ~/.mccode/settings.yaml Your preferences for every project. project <repo>/.microclaw/settings.yaml Shared with the repository. Read only in trusted projects. local <repo>/.microclaw/settings.local.yaml This project, not committed: mccode adds it to the repository's .git/info/exclude when it writes the file. Read only in trusted projects. /permissions add writes here. (The approval dialog's "always allow this command in this project" is kept in ~/.mccode/allow-rules.json; see /allow.) managed /etc/mccode/managed.yaml (macOS: /Library/Application Support/mccode/managed.yaml, Windows: %ProgramData%\mccode\managed.yaml; MCCODE_MANAGED names another file) Set by an administrator. Its values win and its deny / ask rules always apply. The layers merge in that order: user, then project, then local, then managed. For a single value, the later layer wins. Lists are combined instead: permission rules, hooks, domains, writable roots and notification events from every layer all apply. .microclaw/project.yaml keeps working as before; it holds checks, instructions and verification settings. Editors that understand the YAML language server get completion and validation from the schema line at the top of the file: # yaml-language-server: $schema=https://microclaw.ai/schema/code-settings.v1.json version: 1 The schema is also in the repository (docs/schema/code-settings.v1.json) and printed by mccode config schema. Settings files carry a version; mccode config migrate upgrades older files when the format changes.

mccode config # effective settings mccode config get tui.theme # one value and the layer it comes from mccode config set tui.theme github-light mccode config set --layer local permissions.default_mode auto mccode config unset tui.sidebar mccode config paths # files in merge order, which are loaded mccode config doctor # unknown keys, bad rules, bad values mccode config init # commented template (user layer) mccode config edit --layer project # open a layer in $EDITOR, then check it In the TUI, /config, /config get|set|unset|doctor|paths, /permissions, /hooks, /keys and /theme do the same. You can also ask for a change in plain words. For example, /configure use a light theme and ask me before any git push has the model propose concrete changes. You see each one, with the layer it would write to, and nothing is written until you confirm.

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://microclaw.ai/schema/code-settings.v1.json version: 1 model: default: deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro # <profile>/<model> roles: plan: deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro # plan-mode turns review: deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro # /review and mccode review summary: deepseek-flash # compaction summaries and handoffs profiles: deepseek: type: openai # any OpenAI-compatible API base_url: https://api.deepseek.com api_key_env: DEEPSEEK_API_KEY model: deepseek-v4-pro permissions: default_mode: ask allow: - bash(cargo test *) - bash(git status) - edit(src/**) ask: - bash(git push *) - mcp(github.*) deny: - read(**/.env) - bash(rm -rf /*) sandbox: network: ask # off | ask | on allow_domains: [docs.rs, crates.io, "*.github.com"] hooks: pre_tool_use: - matcher: Bash command: ./scripts/guard.sh post_edit: - matcher: Edit|Write command: cargo fmt -- {file} tui: theme: auto screen: auto # auto | fullscreen | inline sidebar: auto # auto | show | hide diff: auto # auto | split | unified status_line: [mode, model, context, tokens, cost, branch] notifications: { method: auto, when: unfocused } keymap: chat.steer: ctrl+s notify: chat: telegram:123456789 events: [approval, done, check_failed]

model.profiles lets MicroClaw Code reach a provider without a full MicroClaw configuration file. If model.default names a profile (and --config is not given), that profile is used instead of config.yaml. Keep API keys in environment variables (api_key_env), or put api_key in the user layer only; mccode config doctor warns about keys in project layers. model.roles picks models for kinds of work: plan for plan-mode turns, review for reviews, summary for compaction summaries and handoffs. A role switches the model within the session's provider, so it must name a model on the same profile (ds/deepseek-v4-pro when the session runs on ds) or a bare model name; a role on another profile is skipped with a warning. Unset roles use the session's model. subagent is accepted but not used yet: sub-agents and explore run on the session's model. /model opens a picker with your profiles and the built-in presets, which list each model's context window.

A rule is <kind>(<pattern>): Kind Matches Pattern bash shell commands Command text; * is a wildcard and git push also matches git push origin main. Commands joined with &&, ||, ;, | are checked one by one: a deny or ask on any part applies, and an allow needs every part to be allowed. read read_file, glob, grep Path glob relative to the project (src/**, **/.env); absolute and ~/ paths work. edit write_file, edit_file, apply_patch Path glob, checked against every file a patch touches. net web_fetch Host, with *.example.com wildcards. mcp MCP tools server.tool glob. agent explore, sub-agents Agent name. tool any tool Tool name glob. Deny wins over ask, and ask wins over allow. deny blocks the call and tells the model why. ask needs your approval, even for tools that normally run without one, and even in auto mode. allow lets shell commands run without asking. Edits outside the project always ask unless an allow rule covers them. Claude Code spellings are accepted too: Bash(npm test), Read(./.env), Edit(src/**), WebFetch(domain:docs.rs), mcp__github__create_issue. sandbox.network controls web access for both shell commands and web tools: Value Shell commands Web tools on Have network access. Run without asking. ask Run without network. Ask for any host not listed in allow_domains. off Run without network. Are denied for any host not listed in allow_domains.

Hooks use the Claude Code protocol, so existing hook scripts work as they are. Input: the event arrives as JSON on stdin, with session_id, cwd, hook_event_name, tool_name and tool_input. Tool names use the Claude spelling (Bash, Edit, Read, …), and microclaw_tool_name holds ours. Blocking: exit code 2 blocks, with stderr as the reason. JSON output: on stdout, a hook can return decision, reason, hookSpecificOutput.permissionDecision (allow / ask / deny), updatedInput, additionalContext, continue and systemMessage. HTTP: set url instead of command to POST the same JSON to an endpoint and read the same JSON back. Event When Can session_start / session_end The TUI starts or exits Show messages user_prompt_submit Before a prompt is sent Block it, add context pre_tool_use Before every tool call, sub-agents included Allow, ask, deny, rewrite the input post_tool_use After every tool call Add context to the result post_edit After each edited file ({file} in the command) Format the file, add context permission_request When an approval would be shown Approve or deny it notification When MicroClaw Code needs you Forward the notification pre_compact Before /compact Block it stop When a turn ends Block, which sends the reason back to the agent once Each handler can set a matcher, a regex on the tool name (either spelling), and a timeout in seconds (default 60). The older hooks.after_edit and hooks.after_turn in project.yaml still run.

Themes. Built in: dark, light, ansi (only the 16 terminal colours), tokyonight, catppuccin, gruvbox, nord, dracula, one-dark, solarized-light, github-light. auto: chooses dark or light from the terminal's background (via COLORFGBG) and defaults to dark. Colour depth: on 256-colour terminals colours are mapped to the nearest palette entry. On 16-colour terminals, or with NO_COLOR, the ansi theme is used. Picking one: /theme previews themes live as you move through the list and saves your choice to the user layer. Custom themes. Put YAML files in ~/.mccode/themes/. OpenCode theme JSON files work in the same directory. name: my-theme base: dark # tokens not set here come from the base palette: blue: "#7aa2f7" tokens: accent: blue background_panel: "#1f2335" diff_added_bg: "#20303b" diff_removed_bg: "#37222c" mode_auto: { dark: "#e0af68", light: "#8f5e15" } syntax_theme: Coldark-Dark A token value is one of: #rrggbb, a 0–255 palette index, a palette name, {dark, light}, or none (use the terminal's own colour). Screen. screen: fullscreen uses the alternate screen and has mouse support: The wheel scrolls. Clicking a tool call expands it. Shift-drag selects text in most terminals. screen: inline writes finished output into the terminal's own scrollback and redraws only the bottom of the screen. auto chooses inline under Zellij and fullscreen otherwise. If a terminal cannot run inline mode, mccode falls back to fullscreen. Other options: sidebar: the side panel (plan, checks, changed files, sub-agents) shows on terminals 130 columns or wider. diff: auto: diffs are shown side by side from 160 columns. animations: false: stops the shimmer effects. status_line: picks and orders the idle status line from mode, model, context, tokens, cost, branch, sandbox, session and checks.

tui.keymap maps an action to one or more keys (ctrl+s, alt+enter, f2, comma-separated), or to none. /keys lists the current bindings. Action Default chat.steer Ctrl+S send now as guidance to the running turn chat.newline Alt+Enter, Shift+Enter, Ctrl+J new line chat.editor Ctrl+G edit the prompt in $EDITOR chat.paste_image Ctrl+V attach the clipboard image history.search Ctrl+R search earlier prompts app.palette Ctrl+P command palette app.mode Shift+Tab plan → ask → auto app.sidebar Ctrl+B show / hide the side panel app.changes F2 review changes hunk by hunk app.clear Ctrl+L clear the screen transcript.pager Ctrl+T whole transcript with search transcript.expand Ctrl+O expand all tool output and diffs

In the terminal. When the terminal is not focused, mccode notifies you on three events: an approval is needed, a turn finished, or checks still fail. Setting Values tui.notifications.method auto (the default), osc9, osc777, bell, off. auto uses OSC 9 for iTerm2, WezTerm, Ghostty and kitty, OSC 777 for VTE terminals, and the bell elsewhere. tui.notifications.when unfocused (the default) or always. These notifications are passed through tmux. In your chat app. If this machine is paired with a MicroClaw Server (mccode remote pair), notify.chat sends approvals and notifications to a Telegram, Discord, Slack or Feishu chat. Each event is sent only when it is listed in notify.events. Approval cards (approval): once the terminal has been idle for after_idle_secs (default 60), an open approval is also sent to the chat as a card with buttons. Answer in the chat or in the terminal; whichever comes first wins. Approval cards go only to the Server's control chats. Other events: done, check_failed and error send a short message. See Run tasks on a MicroClaw Server.

mccode import claude # dry run: what would be imported mccode import claude --apply # into .microclaw/settings.yaml mccode import codex --apply --target user mccode import opencode --apply Source What is imported Claude Code Permission rules and command hooks from ~/.claude/settings.json and .claude/settings*.json, plus .claude/commands, .claude/agents and the servers in .mcp.json. Codex mcp_servers and simple prefix_rules from ~/.codex/rules/*.rules, plus ~/.codex/prompts. OpenCode The permission map, commands, agents, MCP servers and themes. Secrets are never copied into project layers. Anything that cannot be converted is listed as skipped. In the TUI, use /import claude|codex|opencode [apply].

This page covers the day-to-day use of mccode: the terminal interface, permission modes and approvals, the shell sandbox, project trust, verification, sessions, scripting and evaluation. Install and first steps are in Overview and install. Modes, approvals, the sandbox, trust, verification and sessions work the same in Zed; the Zed panel itself is described in Use with Zed.

mccode # full-screen interface mccode "fix the failing parser test" # start with a task mccode -c # continue the most recent session here (shows its history) mccode --session <id> # resume a session (see `mccode sessions`) mccode -p "add a --verbose flag" --mode auto # one task, then exit mccode -p "explain the build" --json # JSON Lines runtime events microclaw code … # same, through the Server binary In the TUI: Key Action Enter send; while the agent works, queue the message for after this turn Ctrl+S send now as guidance to the running turn Up (empty input) take the last queued message back for editing Alt+Enter, Shift+Enter, Ctrl+J, trailing \ new line / and @ command and file pop-ups (fuzzy; ↑↓ choose, Tab / Enter accept) ! (empty input) shell mode: run a command yourself; its output goes to the agent with your next message Shift+Tab cycle mode: plan → ask → auto Esc / Ctrl+C stop the running agent Esc Esc rewind: pick an earlier turn, restore its files and edit its prompt Ctrl+P command palette Ctrl+R search earlier prompts (history is kept per project) Ctrl+G edit the prompt in $EDITOR Ctrl+V attach an image from the clipboard Ctrl+O expand / collapse all tool output and diffs (or click one) Ctrl+T the whole transcript in a pager with / search F2 review the uncommitted changes hunk by hunk Ctrl+B show / hide the side panel PgUp / PgDn, mouse wheel, End scroll the transcript Ctrl+C twice, Ctrl+D, /exit quit Keys can be rebound, and themes, the status line and the screen mode changed, in settings. Large pastes collapse into a [Pasted #1 +120 lines] chip that is expanded when you send. Commands: /help, /mode [plan|ask|auto], /plan [task], /check [name|all], /verify [on|off], /trust, /allow, /diff [full], /new, /sessions, /status, /init, /clear, /exit, and: Command What it does /goal [--until <command>] [--rounds N] <objective> Keep working, round after round, until the goal is met. The agent ends a reply with GOAL COMPLETE (counted only as its last line) when it is done, or with GOAL BLOCKED: <reason> when it needs you. With --until, the goal is reached only when that command succeeds; it runs after every round and its failing output goes into the next one. Without it, the agent's word counts once the project's checks pass. It also stops after two rounds in a row that changed no files, at the round limit (8 by default), or when a turn fails or is cancelled. /goal shows progress and /goal stop ends it. Also in Zed and with -p (see below). /btw <question> Answer a side question in a throwaway copy of the conversation, even while a turn runs; the main session is not changed. /changes (F2) Review the uncommitted changes file by file: revert a single hunk (a backup patch goes to .git/microclaw/reverted/), mark files reviewed, and leave comments that become a prompt for the agent. /undo Restore the files to how they were before the last turn that changed them. The state you leave is checkpointed too. /rewind [id] Pick an earlier turn (also Esc Esc) and restore its files, or restore a checkpoint by id. /review [focus] Review the uncommitted changes (git diff HEAD plus untracked files) with read-only tools and report findings by severity. Also mccode review [focus] for scripts. /model [name|reset] Pick (or switch to) a model for this session. /theme [name] Pick a theme with live preview. /config, /configure <request> Show or change settings; /configure turns a plain-language request into changes you confirm. /permissions, /hooks, /keys Show permission rules, hooks and key bindings; /permissions add allow|ask|deny <rule>. /import claude|codex|opencode Import settings from another coding agent. /queue [clear] Show or clear messages queued while a turn runs. /cost Requests and input/output tokens of this session, per model. /compact [focus] Summarize older messages now; the optional focus says what the summary must keep. /context How full the context window is: tokens used, the automatic-compaction point, and where the tokens go. /handoff <next task> Start a new session from a summary of this one focused on the next task; this session stays as it is. /export [file] Write this session as Markdown (also mccode export [--out file] for the latest session, or mccode --session <id> export). /fork Continue in a copy of the conversation; the original session is kept. After a turn that changed files, ran checks or fetched pages, a summary card shows the files and line counts, check results, the sandbox, any network use, tokens and cost, and the checkpoint to rewind to. On wide terminals a side panel keeps the plan, checks, changed files and running sub-agents in view. Checkpoints are taken at the start of every turn in a shadow git repository inside the Code home (data/checkpoints); they never touch your own .git.

Shell commands (bash, including background processes) run in the operating system's sandbox by default: bubblewrap on Linux and Seatbelt (sandbox-exec) on macOS. They can read the machine, except credential directories (~/.ssh, ~/.gnupg, ~/.aws, ~/.azure, ~/.config/gcloud, ~/.kube, ~/.docker, ~/.netrc, ~/.git-credentials, ~/.microclaw, ~/.mccode). They can write only the repository, the temp directory and common tool caches (~/.cache, ~/.cargo, ~/.rustup, ~/.npm, ~/.gradle, ~/go, …), so builds and tests keep working. Network access is on; --no-network turns it off. With network off, a command in the sandbox cannot change anything outside the repository, so in ask mode such commands run without asking (destructive ones such as git push or rm -rf still ask). On Linux without a working bwrap, Landlock is used instead: writes are confined the same way (and outgoing TCP is blocked on kernels with Landlock ABI 4+), but credential directories stay readable, so commands keep asking. MCCODE_LOCAL_SANDBOX=landlock forces Landlock and MCCODE_LOCAL_SANDBOX=none turns the OS sandbox off; any other value (or none) detects the best one. --review-commands has the model annotate every approval with a one-line verdict; a command it calls DANGEROUS asks you even in auto mode. This is defence in depth: the approval rules above still apply. Turn it off with --sandbox off (or MCCODE_SANDBOX=off). If the machine has no working OS sandbox (no bwrap, or unprivileged user namespaces disabled), Code says so at startup and commands run unsandboxed; mccode doctor reports the state. The MicroClaw Server can use the same mechanism with sandbox: { mode: all, backend: local }.

Mode Behaviour plan Read-only tools; the agent proposes a plan. Approve it to switch to ask and execute. ask (default) File edits apply directly (shown as diffs, with checkpoints); shell commands ask first. auto Shell commands run without asking, except destructive ones (rm -rf, git push, git reset --hard, sudo, curl … | sh, publish, plus your always_ask patterns). Outside plan mode the agent gets the workspace tool set (ToolPolicy::WorkspaceWrite): file, search, shell, planning, sub-agent and MCP tools, without channel delivery, scheduling, A2A or media tools. In the TUI an approval pauses the agent in place: the dialog's answer goes back into the same run (approve once, always allow the tool in this session, deny — the agent sees the denial and continues). For shell commands it also offers always allow <command prefix> in this project (key p), for example cargo test. Such a rule covers only single simple commands that start with the prefix (cargo test -p x, but never cargo test && …, pipes, redirections or $(…)); interpreters, sudo, rm, curl and the like cannot be allowed by prefix, and the destructive list above still asks. Rules live in ~/.mccode/allow-rules.json; manage them with /allow [list | add <prefix> | rm <prefix>] or mccode allow [list | add | remove]. In -p mode an approval that needs a person ends the run with exit code 2; resume it with mccode --session <id> -p 1 (approve once) or -p 3 (deny). Exit codes: 0 done, 1 failed / cancelled / checks still failing, 2 approval pending. mccode -p "/goal [--until <command>] [--rounds N] <objective>" runs a goal without a person: every round prints as usual, the last line says how it ended, and the exit code is 1 when the goal was not reached. With --json the result line carries "goal": {"reached", "rounds", "summary"}. mccode -p "/goal --until 'cargo test' make the parser accept trailing commas" --mode auto

.microclaw/project.yaml lives in the repository and can set the mode, add instructions and define check commands, so it only takes effect once you trust the project — for the exact file content you trusted. If the file changes later (for example after a pull), Code asks again. The TUI asks on first use; in -p mode pass --trust; change the decision with mccode trust [--revoke] or /trust. Untrusted projects ignore the file and never run checks automatically (checks execute the repository's own build scripts). Trusted projects also load the repository's AGENTS.md (or CLAUDE.md, AGENT.md; the first one found, up to 16 KB) into the agent's instructions. In an untrusted project the agent is only told that the file exists.

Checks are detected for Rust, Node (npm/pnpm/yarn/bun scripts), Python (ruff/pytest/mypy), Go and Makefiles, or configured in .microclaw/project.yaml. In trusted projects, when a turn changed the working tree — through the file tools or through shell commands — the auto checks run; a failure goes back to the agent (up to max_fix_rounds, default 2) with an explicit instruction not to weaken tests. mccode info # detected project, trust, checks, config sources mccode check # run all checks mccode check build # run one mccode init # write .microclaw/project.yaml mccode doctor # validate the configuration and start the engine once .microclaw/project.yaml: mode: ask verify: true max_fix_rounds: 2 checks: - name: build run: cargo check --all-targets auto: true - name: test run: cargo test always_ask: - terraform apply instructions: | Use pnpm, not npm. compact_instructions: Keep the names of public APIs and any open TODOs. lsp: true max_session_tokens: 3000000 hooks: after_edit: - cargo fmt

The status bar shows how full the model's context window is (ctx 42%; yellow from 70%, red from 85%), and /context breaks it down. Code measures every request against the model's window (known models are recognized by name; set model_context_windows in the model config for others) and, from 80% of it: clears older tool outputs first (the newest ~40k tokens of output stay; a file read again later replaces the earlier read), then summarizes older history into fixed sections (goal and constraints, decisions, files and state, errors and fixes, plan, verification, next step), keeping your own earlier messages verbatim and the list of files changed. The last ~24k tokens of the conversation stay as they are. If summarizing fails, a mechanical digest is kept; history is never dropped silently, and the full conversation is archived before every compaction. A notice in the transcript (and on stderr with -p) says when it happened. /compact <focus> compacts now and tells the summary what matters; compact_instructions in .microclaw/project.yaml does the same for every compaction in the project.

The agent can hand wide investigations ("where is the retry policy set and who calls it?") to explore, a read-only helper with its own context. Only the helper's short report, with file paths and line numbers, enters the main conversation, and several explore calls run in parallel. Trusted projects can add focused helpers in .microclaw/agents/<name>.md: --- description: Knows the storage layer and its migrations model: claude-haiku-4-5 # optional --- You explain how the database code in crates/storage works. … The model also sees how full its context is on every request, so it can delegate or wrap up before compaction is needed. With --context-tools (or context_tools: true in the project file) it can additionally save checkpoints (context_note) and rewind its own context to one with a note to itself (rewind_context), dropping failed attempts. Files are not reverted.

In trusted projects the agent keeps durable lessons about the repository in .microclaw/memory.md (how to build and test it, slow tests, pitfalls), edits it with the normal file tools (so you see every change as a diff), and reads it at the start of every session. Edit or delete it like any file.

A Markdown file defines a slash command; its body is the prompt and $ARGUMENTS is replaced by what follows the command: --- description: Fix a GitHub issue --- Fix issue #$ARGUMENTS: read it with `gh issue view`, write a failing test first, then fix it. Put personal commands in ~/.mccode/commands/ and project commands in .microclaw/commands/ (trusted projects only; they win on a name clash). /help lists them, Tab completes them, and mccode -p "/fix-issue 42" runs one non-interactively.

When the agent changed files, MicroClaw Code asks the language server of each file's language for errors before running the checks: rust-analyzer, typescript-language-server, pyright-langserver or gopls, whichever is installed. Errors are handed back like a failed check (lsp), usually faster and more precisely than a full build. Language servers run project code (build scripts), so this needs a trusted project; lsp: false turns it off. Hooks run shell commands in the project root at fixed points (trusted projects only): hooks: after_edit: # after the agent changed files, before the checks - cargo fmt after_turn: # when a turn that changed files ends - ./scripts/notify.sh A failing hook is reported but does not stop the turn.

Mention an image file with @ (@docs/screenshot.png, an absolute path or ~/…; PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP up to 5 MB) and it is sent to the model with the prompt, for example a screenshot of a broken layout or an error dialog. Drag a file into the terminal to paste its path. In Zed, images pasted into the agent panel are attached the same way. The model must support images.

mccode -p "add retries to the HTTP client" --mode auto --worktree retries mccode -p "update the README examples" --mode auto --worktree docs & mccode worktree list mccode worktree remove retries --worktree [name] runs the session in a new git worktree on branch mccode/<name> (under ~/.mccode/worktrees), so several tasks can run at once without touching your checkout or each other. When it ends, Code prints the branch, its commits and how to review, merge or remove it. Trust carries over from the main checkout.

mccode review --pr 123 # review the PR's diff, print findings mccode review --pr 123 "error handling" --post # …and post them as a PR comment The diff comes from the GitHub CLI (gh pr diff) or, without it, from origin's refs/pull/123/head. The review runs with read-only tools. --post uses gh pr comment and is the only step that writes to GitHub.

--max-session-tokens 2000000 (or max_session_tokens in the project file) stops a session before the next request once it has used that many tokens (input + output, all models), with a notice; -p exits with status 1.

Windows has no OS sandbox for shell commands yet. Commands run with your permissions, ask mode asks before every command, and Code warns when you use auto mode without a sandbox. Prefer ask mode in repositories you do not trust, or use WSL, where the Linux sandbox applies.

The agent can drive REPLs and debuggers: it starts one with bash run_in_background, sends input with bash_input and reads output with bash_output. Input goes to stdin without a terminal, so line-oriented modes work best (python3 -u -i, node -i, gdb -q). Background processes are stopped when the session ends.

mccode -p "update the changelog for the new flag" --mode auto --trust mccode -p "explain the build" --json > events.jsonl mccode review "error handling" > review.md -p prints the final answer (or, with --json, one runtime event per line) and exits with 0 done, 1 failed / cancelled / checks still failing, 2 approval pending. --trust trusts the project (saved, like mccode trust) so its checks execute; without it an untrusted project runs no checks. --no-verify skips checks, --no-network turns off network access for shell commands, --sandbox off disables the OS sandbox.

mccode eval apps/microclaw-code/eval/cases # PASS/FAIL per case mccode --json eval my-cases --filter parser # JSON Lines mccode eval replay v0.10.0..HEAD --check "cargo test" --out eval/replay A case is a directory with case.yaml (prompt, check, optional setup, mode, timeout_secs) and a repo/ snapshot. Each case runs in a fresh git repository in auto mode with verification; the case passes when check exits 0 afterwards. eval replay turns bug-fix commits into cases (parent commit = snapshot, commit message = prompt), a regression set built from real history. Results include duration, requests and tokens.

MicroClaw supports the following slash commands in chat channels. Supported channels: Telegram, Discord, Slack, Feishu/Lark, IRC.

Command Description /clear Clear current chat context (session + chat history) but keep scheduled tasks for that chat. /reset Clear current chat context (session + chat history) and remove scheduled tasks for that chat. /reset memory Clear current chat memory (chat AGENTS.md + structured memories) without clearing conversation or tasks. /stop Abort the active run in the current chat. Does not clear session or chat history. /skills List all currently available skills discovered by runtime. /rewind List the most recent filesystem checkpoints for the current chat (newest first). Requires checkpoints_enabled: true. /rewind <commit> Restore the chat's working directory to the given checkpoint hash. Hash must be 4–64 hex chars. /reload-skills Reload skills from disk and return the reloaded count. /archive Archive current in-memory session as a markdown conversation file. /usage Show usage and memory observability summary for current chat. /status Show current provider/model (effective for this bot account) and current-chat status summary. /providers List configured provider profiles and indicate the active one. /provider Show current provider/model. /provider <profile> switches the current bot account to that provider profile and persists it to config. /provider reset clears the current bot account override. /models List configured models for the active provider. /models api fetches the live provider model list when supported. /model Show current provider/model. /model <name> switches the current bot account model override and persists it to config. /model reset clears the current bot account override.

Any input starting with / is treated as a command. Inputs with leading mentions before slash are also treated as commands (for example @bot /status, <@U123> /status). Commands are matched exactly (for example, /reset). Chat commands such as /reset, /clear, /stop, /usage, and /archive are scoped to the current chat conversation. /provider and /model are scoped to the current bot account, not all bots on the same channel type. Slash command inputs are not appended to agent conversation history/session context. Unknown slash commands return Unknown command.. /stop only aborts in-flight work for the current chat; it does not clear context. In group/server/channel chats, slash commands are mention-gated by default. To disable mention-gating for group slash commands, set allow_group_slash_without_mention: true. /archive is manual; automatic archive may also happen before context compaction. /provider and /model changes are persisted into microclaw.config.yaml for the current bot/account, so they survive restart.

subagents.acp supports two patterns: inline default worker: configure enabled, command, and args named workers: configure targets and optionally default_target Example: subagents: acp: enabled: true default_target: "reviewer" targets: reviewer: enabled: true command: codex args: ["--model", "gpt-5.4"] fast-fix: enabled: true command: codex args: ["--model", "gpt-5.3-codex"] auto_approve: false Resolution order for sessions_spawn(runtime="acp"): explicit runtime_target subagents.acp.default_target inline subagents.acp.command the only enabled named target, if exactly one exists If multiple named targets are enabled and no default is set, MicroClaw returns a configuration error and asks for runtime_target.

Use these keys when a provider/model needs extra OpenAI-compatible request body parameters. Merge order (later wins): openai_compat_body_overrides (global) openai_compat_body_overrides_by_provider[llm_provider] openai_compat_body_overrides_by_model[model] Set a value to null to remove that key from the outgoing JSON body. llm_provider: "deepseek" model: "deepseek-chat" openai_compat_body_overrides: temperature: 0.2 max_tokens: 4096 openai_compat_body_overrides_by_provider: deepseek: top_p: null reasoning_effort: "high" openai_compat_body_overrides_by_model: deepseek-chat: temperature: 0.0 Behavior details: provider keys are normalized to lowercase during config load model keys are trim-normalized and matched by exact model string runtime-controlled fields such as stream mode and tool payload can still be set by MicroClaw depending on request path

The global llm_provider + api_key + model act as the main profile. If you need a channel or bot to use a different provider, key, base URL, or model, define a reusable provider_presets.<id> profile and point channels.<name>.provider_preset or channels.<name>.accounts.<id>.provider_preset at it. openai_compat_body_overrides_by_model still matches against the effective model chosen by that profile. For a single bot/account model override without changing the shared preset, set channels.<name>.accounts.<id>.model. Slash commands follow the same scope: /provider and /model persist to the current bot/account fields, not to all bots sharing the same provider preset. llm_provider: "anthropic" api_key: "sk-ant-..." model: "claude-sonnet-4-5-20250929" # global main profile provider_presets: ops-openrouter: provider: "openrouter" api_key: "sk-or-..." llm_base_url: "https://openrouter.ai/api/v1" # optional; defaults from provider matrix llm_user_agent: "microclaw-ops/1.0" # optional default_model: "openai/gpt-4o-mini" show_thinking: false deepseek-ops: provider: "deepseek" api_key: "sk-ds-..." default_model: "deepseek/deepseek-chat" channels: telegram: provider_preset: "ops-openrouter" default_account: "main" accounts: main: enabled: true bot_token: "xxx" ops: enabled: true bot_token: "yyy" provider_preset: "deepseek-ops" model: "deepseek/deepseek-chat" openai_compat_body_overrides: temperature: 0.2 openai_compat_body_overrides_by_model: "openai/gpt-4o-mini": temperature: 0.0 "deepseek/deepseek-chat": top_p: null reasoning_effort: "high" Notes: llm_provider + global api_key + model act as the main profile. provider_presets are the supported reusable LLM profile surface for channels/bots. channels.<name>.accounts.<id>.model is the bot/account-local model override surface. If two bots share the same model string, they share the same by_model override block.

To run bash tool calls in containers, set: sandbox: mode: "all" backend: "auto" # auto|docker|podman security_profile: "hardened" # hardened|standard|privileged # cap_add: ["SETUID", "SETGID", "CHOWN"] image: "ubuntu:25.10" container_prefix: "microclaw-sandbox" no_network: true require_runtime: true Behavior: sandbox.mode: "off" (default): host execution. sandbox.security_profile defaults to hardened: hardened: --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges (most restrictive) standard: Docker default capabilities (useful when sandbox commands need apt/chown/su) privileged: full container privilege (--privileged), debugging only sandbox.cap_add appends --cap-add entries for hardened and standard. Runtime backend selection: backend: "auto": Docker only (backward-compatible default behavior) backend: "docker": Docker only backend: "podman": Podman only sandbox.mode: "all" + configured runtime unavailable: require_runtime: false: fallback to host with warning. require_runtime: true: fail fast. Quick opt-in: microclaw setup --enable-sandbox microclaw doctor sandbox Optional hardening files: mount allowlist: ~/.microclaw/sandbox-mount-allowlist.txt file path allowlist: ~/.microclaw/sandbox-path-allowlist.txt Each file supports one absolute path per line (# comments allowed).

channels.<name>.bot_username is optional for all channels. If set, it overrides global bot_username for that channel. Telegram enabled: At least one enabled channels.telegram.accounts.<id>.bot_token Discord enabled: At least one enabled channels.discord.accounts.<id>.bot_token Slack enabled: At least one enabled channels.slack.accounts.<id> with both bot_token and app_token Feishu/Lark enabled: At least one enabled account with channels.feishu.accounts.<id>.app_id and channels.feishu.accounts.<id>.app_secret IRC enabled: channels.irc.server, channels.irc.nick, and channels.irc.channels are required. documents.t: Memory is stored in AGENTS.md files under ~/.microclaw/runtime/groups/ by default (or under your configured data_dir) and injected into the system prompt for every request. There are three scopes: global (groups/AGENTS.md), bot/account (groups/{channel}/AGENTS.md), and chat (groups/{channel}/{chat_id}/AGENTS.md).
The scheduler polls every 60 seconds for due tasks, runs the same agent loop as normal messages, sends the result, and updates the next run time.

This page documents the webhook-style HTTP trigger surface for external automation. Use this when you want CI jobs, webhook handlers, or cron scripts to trigger MicroClaw runs without opening Web UI.

By default, request sessionKey is blocked (hooks_allow_request_session_key: false). If enabled, hooks_allowed_session_key_prefixes can restrict allowed values. If request sessionKey is missing, MicroClaw uses hooks_default_session_key.

OpenClaw-style payload shape is supported: { "message": "Summarize inbox", "name": "Email", "sessionKey": "hook:email:msg-123" } Behavior: message is required. name is optional and used as sender fallback. accepted requests start an async run and return run_id. Use GET /api/stream?run_id=<id> to consume events.
Payload: { "text": "New email received", "mode": "now" } text is required. mode is optional: now (default): starts async run immediately. next-heartbeat: queues a system-event message only.

Rust 1.70+ (2021 edition) — only required for building from source; the installer ships prebuilt binaries macOS, Linux, or Windows Internet access for chat + your selected LLM provider API Minimum hardware: 1 vCPU / 1 GB RAM — microclaw is a single Rust binary with embedded SQLite, so it runs comfortably on a $5/month VPS (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Vultr, etc.). The prebuilt Linux binaries are dynamically linked against glibc 2.39 (the ubuntu-latest build toolchain) and OpenSSL 3 (libssl.so.3). They run only on a distribution whose system glibc is 2.39 or newer. On an older system you will see errors such as: microclaw: error while loading shared libraries: libssl.so.3: cannot open shared object file microclaw: /lib64/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.39' not found (required by microclaw) Distribution glibc Status Ubuntu 24.04 LTS+ 2.39 ✅ works Debian 13 (trixie)+ 2.41 ✅ works AlmaLinux / Rocky / RHEL 10+ 2.39 ✅ works Fedora 40+ 2.39 ✅ works Debian 12 (bookworm) 2.36 ❌ too old AlmaLinux / RHEL 8–9 2.28–2.34 ❌ too old Ubuntu 22.04 / 20.04 2.35 / 2.31 ❌ too old Check your version with ldd --version. If you only hit the libssl.so.3 error (glibc is new enough), just install the OpenSSL 3 runtime — dnf install openssl3-libs on RHEL-family, apt install libssl3 on Debian/Ubuntu. If glibc is too old, either run on a supported release (Ubuntu 24.04 / AlmaLinux 10), use a newer container base image, or build from source. A static build via the x86_64-unknown-linux-musl target removes both the glibc and OpenSSL system dependencies.

Learning Foundry turns a user-selected direction into a recurring, governed learning programme. It complements long-horizon learning: long-horizon learning distils evidence from work the agent already performed; Learning Foundry proactively researches an explicit capability gap during a bounded background epoch. It does not fine-tune the model or let a research run rewrite live policy.

A learning track contains an objective, concrete directions, an allowlist of source domains or source classes, a six-field cron schedule and IANA timezone, per-epoch token and source-count budgets, and a promotion mode. The runtime checks due tracks once per minute. Before an epoch starts it moves the next-run timestamp forward, so duplicate scheduler ticks cannot run the same epoch. The shared agent loop then performs a read-only research task. Its prompt treats retrieved material as untrusted evidence and prohibits credential use, external mutations, live-skill edits, and execution of downloaded code. A separate curator call may turn the report into one candidate. A valid candidate must include a portable Agent Skills name, operational Markdown instructions, dated source URLs, at least three self-contained validation scenarios, and a risk classification. Candidate instructions pass the shared prompt-injection scanner. Candidates remain inert; they are not included in skill discovery or prompts.

Every new candidate enters an automatic paired evaluation before it can be promoted. Each declared scenario is run twice against the same model: the baseline arm receives only the scenario; the candidate arm receives the same scenario plus the proposed skill. These calls deliberately have no tool schema. They cannot access the network, filesystem, credentials, shell, MCP, channel delivery, or live skills. A separate conservative verifier applies the scenario's expected and forbidden criteria to both responses. Candidate text and responses are passed as untrusted data, not authority. The database records paired pass/fail results, response excerpts, token counts, durations, and regression count. The initial gate requires at least three completed samples, zero baseline-pass/candidate-fail regressions, and strictly more candidate passes than baseline passes. An infrastructure or verifier error fails closed. Operators may rerun a failed evaluation, but cannot bypass it during promotion. This stage is an isolated behavioral simulation, not proof that a procedure can successfully mutate a real external system. Tool-bearing workflows still need the existing paired Shadow/Canary substrate before any future automatic activation policy is enabled.

The learning_tracks tool supports create, list, pause, resume, archive, and run_now. { "action": "create", "chat_id": 42, "name": "rust-runtime-reliability", "objective": "Learn repeatable ways to diagnose and recover Rust agent runtimes", "directions": ["Tokio task recovery", "SQLite crash consistency"], "allowed_sources": ["doc.rust-lang.org", "docs.rs", "github.com/tokio-rs"], "schedule": "0 0 3 * * *", "timezone": "America/Los_Angeles", "token_budget": 80000, "max_sources": 20, "promotion_mode": "propose" } Tracks, epochs, candidates, and evaluation summaries are returned by GET /api/learning_observability. An administrator can promote a reviewed new-skill candidate only after its isolated evaluation passes. A failed candidate can be reevaluated with: POST /api/learning/tracks/candidates/evaluate Content-Type: application/json {"session_key":"main","candidate_id":"..."} Promotion uses: POST /api/learning/tracks/candidates/promote Content-Type: application/json {"session_key":"main","candidate_id":"..."} Promotion rejects a candidate whose name already belongs to a live skill. Changes to an existing skill must use comparative reflection and paired shadow evidence, preserving the active version as the baseline. Promotion materializes the file but registers its lifecycle as candidate, not trusted. Real task outcomes therefore act as the Canary stage through the existing skill-governance policy: verified success can advance candidate → trial → trusted, while repeated failures degrade it and restore a previous trusted version when one exists. The isolated evaluator is a prerequisite for this Canary; it does not replace outcome evidence.

Research and curation are separate model calls. No candidate is auto-activated. Source text is evidence, never authority. A candidate requires provenance and tests. Promotion fails closed unless paired isolated evaluation passed. Evaluation runs with no tools, network, filesystem, or credentials. Baseline/candidate regressions, token use, and latency are persisted. Injection scanning runs before storage and again before promotion. Only an admin-scoped API can promote a candidate. Existing skills cannot be overwritten through this path. Epoch failures and abstentions remain observable. Restarting does not lose tracks, epoch history, or candidates. Learning Foundry optimizes reusable task behavior only. Tool guardrails, filesystem/network policies, hooks, and channel authorization remain authoritative.
